claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
Ease of dislocation motion governs the low hardness and strength of the stated CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Stacking-fault formation governs the low hardness and strength of the stated CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
In-situ TEM can directly reveal stacking-fault formation during deformation.
In-situ TEM can directly establish the ease of dislocation motion during deformation.
Synchrotron X-ray diffraction can directly observe the proposed dislocation-motion and stacking-fault mechanisms.
Mechanical-property and deformation testing will produce a 10–20% decrease in hardness and strength relative to the starting state.
The hypothesis applies to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The hypothesis is limited to a simple solid-solution structural state.
The proposed loading domain is mechanical-property and deformation testing.
The exact dislocation-motion and stacking-fault mechanism is not fully understood.
A lack of correlation between dislocation or stacking-fault observations and the predicted property decrease would falsify the hypothesis.
A 5% difference between predicted and observed values is the falsification threshold.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis seeks to explain low properties already present in the starting state, but the stated intervention is only an observational characterization method while the predicted outcome is a further 10–20% property decrease. No material-changing intervention is defined that could cause this decrease.

The structural mediator names candidate deformation processes, whereas the mechanism merely states that those processes will be observed; observation is not a causal mechanism linking them to low hardness or strength.
